utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. PRESIDING OFFICER: Defence for Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Please tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: My first name is Djoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about your last name?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: It's Lazic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When were you born, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 3rd of April, 1955.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you born, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Tutnjevac, municipality of Ugljevik, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lazic, please tell us: What schooling do you have?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: I've completed secondary religious school in the monastery in 1975, and then I graduated from the faculty of theology in 1982, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Father, please tell us: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm married, and I believe myself to be happily married, and I have three children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you serve your military service?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: I completed my military service in 1981 in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us about your work. Where are you employed?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: The first employment was in Tuzla, and starting on the 4th November of 1985, I've been working in Milosevac in Modrica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: How far is Milosevac from Samac?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: Milosevac is a village in Posavina, somewhere halfway between Modrica and Samac, so eight kilometres to Samac and eight kilometres to Modrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us: Prior to April 1992, what area did your parish cover?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: My parish covered two villages: Kruskovo Polje, which belonged to Samac municipality; and village of Milosevac, which belonged to Modrica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As I understood it, you are residing in the village of Milosevac.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've been residing there since 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Father, please tell us: Do you know Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: Upon my arrival from Tuzla to work in Milosevac as a priest, one of the first people I met in Samac -- in the very early days of my arrival to that parish, I felt great attachment to Samac, and one of the first people I met there was Mr. Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Father, please tell us: Immediately prior to April of 1992, and throughout 1991, did you frequent Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: I have to say that two establishments that I used to frequent in Samac were Cafe AS and a seafood restaurant whose owner was a Muslim, a Bosniak, named Hamid. And the reason I went to Cafe AS was that it has been recommended to me by my neighbour. Mr. Miroslav Tadic was a teacher and was a renowned intellectual in the area, and he was quite popular with his students. All of the students, to this day, speak very favourably about him. And this neighbour of mine was also his student, and he recommended that I go there. I always felt very comfortable there and I frequent that place even nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me how frequently, prior to the conflict, you went to Cafe AS.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: At least twice a week, on a Wednesday and on a Saturday, because there was a green market held on Wednesday and we used to gather there. We had a company of people that gathered there. And then there were some weeks when I would go there several times a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Father, please tell me: What was the ethnic composition of patrons of the Cafe AS at the time when you used to go there?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: With your permission, let me just say something else. Before me, another priest worked in Samac. His name is Djoko as well. He's a relative of mine and he's in Belgrade now. And when I came to Samac, some people confused me with the other priest Djoko. And when I came there, I said that I was a different Father Djoko. People accepted me, welcomed me, in that area. There were Serbs and Croats and Muslims there, and they said that I needed to continue the tradition of the previous priest, my relative, who was very friendly with them, and that I needed to continue socialising with them, which I did. And there were many young people in that company, and there were many Serbs and Muslims and Croats among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, please tell us: Prior to April 1992, were there any premises in Cafe AS which were not accessible to all patrons? Or rather, can you tell us: How many rooms with the Cafe AS have?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: I know this for a fact, that there were never any rooms which were off limits. There was a total of two rooms. One was for the pool. I personally don't shoot pool, but I used to cheer people playing there. So there were two rooms. One was for the pool, and the other room was where they played cards, various card games and so on. And never once did it occur to anyone to put any of the rooms off limits to anybody. Everybody could go into any of the two rooms whenever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, sir: What was the atmosphere like in the Cafe AS while you went there? Were there any incidents?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: I can assure you that while I was present there, there were no incidents whatsoever. People were just joking while shooting pool, playing cards. We joked. It was a very friendly atmosphere. People enjoyed being together, laughed together, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, please tell us whether you heard, prior to April 1992, about the existence of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about the time after April 1992? Have you heard of its existence after that?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: Later on, I heard from some of my friends from Milosevac that there had been such a detachment, the 4th Detachment, which had a mixed ethnic composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us: Do you know where the headquarters of the 4th Detachment was?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us: While you went to Cafe AS prior to April 1992, did you see any military meetings being held at the Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: No. As a priest, I can assure you - and I claim this with full certainty - that at least while I was there, there were no political or military meetings held there. There were no uniformed people -- members of units in uniform assembling there. People simply had a good time shooting pool, drinking, joking, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us: During the night between the 16th and 17th of April, did you meet or did you perhaps hear of any members of the special units from Serbia wearing camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: After the conflict broke out, I heard about that, and I later even had an occasion to meet the late Lugar. But prior to that, I have never seen them, nor did I know that they existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: After the 17th of April, some of the people that you later learned were members of special units, did you see them ever at the Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: No. I claim with full certainty that I would have known of those people had they frequented Cafe AS. All of the people that I met at the Cafe AS were the people familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether a certain Hasan Ibralic used to come to Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: I don't know that man. I didn't used to see him at the Cafe AS. And since I didn't work at the state-owned companies, nor did I go there, I don't know the man. I don't know what his job was. I just don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps ever see Enes and Nijaz Alatovic?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: No. I never saw them at the Cafe AS. I don't even know those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps see Mehmed Vukovic there?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know him either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Miroslav Tadic was a kum at the church in Dubica prior to the breakout of conflict in Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. I was present, together with the priest Bogdan Tolic from Modrica, and I collected donations when Patriarch Pavle blessed that church. And after the completion of the church service, I congratulated him, and I was very pleased to see him, as a friend of mine, at the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us: What does it mean to be a kum of the church?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: That means that he, by donating a certain amount of money, becomes a kum to the church, or rather, a patron of the church, and thereby he has a duty to bring a special religious cake and to bring a candle to the church, in order to celebrate the patron saint of that church.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So this is some kind of a distinction, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's a very special distinction that he held. Our people usually say that sacred are the people who are kums to the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that when that church was sanctified, Patriarch Pavle was there as well?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. He attended that ceremony as well. All of us had our duties during that ceremony, and I, together with the priest from Modrica, collected donations and a very solemn church service was held during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Father. I have no further questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Lazic, my name is Di Fazio. I've got just a few questions for you. How long had you been living in Bosanski Samac, or in the area, I should say, prior to April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: I've just said a minute ago that I came to the Posavina region from Tuzla on the 4th of November, 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And from that time, had you been frequenting Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: Yes, as early as 1986. I have said that, owing to my neighbour, who was a student of Miroslav Tadic, I had the pleasure to meet him, and he's an intellectual, a good Christian. And because of that, I went to his cafe. I also went to this other restaurant, which was a seafood restaurant, and it's very good seafood, and I used to go to that place, especially during Lent time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And you kept abreast of events in Bosanski Samac, particularly in early 1992, trying to keep yourself informed of what was going on in the community?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: No. I was not informed, either about the political or any other situations. I simply went to Samac as a guest, in order to play cards and have a drink with my friends, hear a joke, laugh a little bit. And then following that, I would return to my parish in Milosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. So your sole connection with Bosanski Samac was to go along to Cafe AS and entertain yourself there?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And in all the time that you were doing that, your evidence is that you never heard of and you never saw any members of any organisation called the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: No. I claim this with full responsibility, that as far as the military organisations are concerned, I heard, neither in Modrica or in Samac, where the headquarters were, I didn't hear anything about how it was organised. I am a priest. I had a lot of work. And when I had some free time, I would go and spend some time with my friends, have a drink, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you continue to frequent Cafe AS after the 16th and 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: It so happened that I was, on the 16th of April, at the AS cafe. I had my coffee, and then following that, I went to the seafood restaurant, because it was Lent time and people were fasting. Upon the breakout of the conflict, I had to attend a funeral, on the 17th, and on the 16th, in the afternoon, I had a traffic accident. And my car remained in Samac, with Tomo Zarak. I didn't know about this. And then on the 17th, people woke me up because there was a funeral in Milosevac. The late Milija [phoen] Tomic had died and I had to attend and hold a service at the funeral. And then there I heard that there had been a conflict in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I was actually concerned with more the weeks and months after the 16th of April, 1992. In the weeks and months after that period of time, did you still go to Cafe AS from time to time?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the 16th of April, the cafes were not open. They were not operating, because there had been an order, both in Modrica and in my village, Milosevac, and in Samac, and therefore, cafes and restaurants did not work. And it wasn't until later that I went there from time to time, because there was shelling and it was quite dangerous. But I still went there, and I do so nowadays as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. What period of time was it that you started going there again?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: Well, in 1992, in the autumn -- or rather, starting in May, when the cafe -- from May, the cafe would be open from time to time, and I used to go occasionally, but not as often as I did before the breakout of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Fine. Of course. And in those troubled times, was it still possible to get a drink at the Cafe AS, post-April 1992?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was possible. One could get a drink at a cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So you're not aware of any order prohibiting the sale of alcohol or consumption of alcohol in the municipality of Bosanski Samac after April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: You said a drink, and I consider juice to be a drink as well, at least in my language. I am a teetotaller. I don't drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You may not. What about others?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: I socialised mostly with people who drink exclusively juices or colas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, but the favourite drink of some of my friends was the homemade plum brandy, slivovitz, so I saw two of my friends drinking that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And in the period of time after the 16th and 17th of April, on these occasions when you started to go back to Cafe AS from time to time, did you then become aware of the existence of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: I heard later that the 4th Detachment -- and I learned of it after the end of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I've got no further questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wish to ask you something in connection with what the Prosecutor asked you. When you spoke about your visit to the Cafe AS after the 16th and 17th of April, if I understood you well, you said that you used to go there after -- or rather, in the fall, in the autumn, but then you also mentioned the month of May. So can you just please be more specific and clarify: When did you actually start going to Cafe AS again, and when was the prohibition in force?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: I was not clear, perhaps. I said that on the 16th, in the afternoon, I had a traffic accident with my car, a Lada, and I left my car in Samac. And then after five days I regained my car, or I went to get my car, and the first stop in Samac was Cafe AS. And I asked Mr. Tadic to show me where the auto mechanic shop was, because this is where my car had been. So after the 16th of April, I went to Cafe AS, not frequently, but I still went to that place. Even though the cafe itself was closed, it wasn't working. There was a spot or a platform in front of it where one -- where people gathered. So the cafe itself wasn't, strictly speaking, working, but I would go to the spot in front of the cafe and see people there and have a drink there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So during that period of time -- May, June, April - Cafe AS, in fact, wasn't working?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't working at the time, because there had been an order issued to that effect. But I still went there to see my friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the people that you mentioned, did you see them in autumn, after Cafe AS started working again, or was it at a different time?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? Other people, my friends?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned some friends and you spoke about two of your friends who liked plum brandy. When did you start seeing them again? Was it in the fall, on that fall of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DJOKO LAZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, in the fall of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you, Mr. Lazic, for coming today. Your deposition is concluded. You may go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Ten minutes' break. --- Break taken at 9.28 a.m. --- Upon resuming at 9.43 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Cordasevic. Will you please tell us your full name, first and last.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Ljubo Cordasevic, born on the 12th of May, 1946, Velika Obarska [phoen], near Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Where are you living now?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I'm living in Samac now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm happily married and the father of two daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: For how long have your ancestors been living in the territory of Samac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I'm in Samac since 1986, and before that, within the territory of Samac municipality, since the 1960s.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I meant your parents, your grandparents.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Bijeljina, and that is where I was educated. I got married in 1967, and since then my whole family has been living in the territory of Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cordasevic, you completed your secondary education in Bijeljina, and higher school for teachers' training in Tuzla, and the faculty of philosophy, in 1982, in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And your occupation is teacher of psychology and pedagogy?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: After 1967, you worked as a teacher in the village of Gornja Slatina, and after 1986, you started working in the centre for social welfare in Samac, and as a psychologist, pedagogist?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Also, in the period after 1980, you worked as a part-time correspond for the newspaper Sport and for other newspapers, such as Oslobodjenje, Sportske Novosti, and others?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Were you a member of any party?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Until the beginning of the armed conflict, which means about 1991, up to 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: After that, after the beginning of the armed conflict, I was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have a position now in that party?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Just now, not a very significant one. I'm a member of the municipal board of the Serbian Democratic Party of Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough and tell us whether you have any position in the field of sports.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Just now, I'm a member of the highest-level bodies of the football association of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cordasevic, you served in the Yugoslav People's Army in 1971, in Nasice, that is right, and you completed your military service in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cordasevic, there's no dispute that at the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, there was a heightening of tension in Samac municipality between members of different ethnic groups. Tell us, please: What is your understanding of that situation? What is your knowledge as to how this occurred and what you experienced yourself?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: In very brief terms: Being of the profession that I am, that is, a pedagogue and a psychologist, it was not difficult to conclude that people in town were not socialising and conversing in the way they used to before. Secondly, I think that these tensions, in my view, were increased and climaxed after the beginning of the war in neighbouring Croatia. And after the multiparty elections, and in the process of the formation of parties, contributed to this atmosphere, and one could conclude from all this that something would soon be happening in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that, as a social worker, you moved around all the places within the territory of Samac. Immediately prior to the outbreak of conflict, did you see patrols in villages held by people of different ethnicities, depending on the population of the village?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: My job was such that I was busy day and night, so I spent a lot of time visiting families to provide care and social welfare. And true that as I moved around, I came across unknown persons, particularly passing through certain villages, such as Hrasnica, Grebnice. I remember well, one night as I was travelling, I was stopped. They asked for my documents. People were not in uniform. They were civilians. I was not mistreated; I was just checked out - that is, my identity was checked out - and the reason that I had no problems is certainly the fact that I was very well known in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now move on to a different topic. Tell us, please: Where were you in the night between the 16th and 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: In that, let us call it, critical night, I was in my own apartment in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I was in my apartment in Samac, and without expecting anything special to happen. I wasn't informed that anything was in the offing, and I stayed in the apartment for four or five days, without anyone calling me or disturbing me, and this applies to all the other inhabitants in the town of Samac. I noticed that something was going on, that something was changing, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: But did you hear shooting that night, that something was actually happening?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question? I didn't hear you too well, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What did you hear during the night between the 16th and the 17th? Did you hear arms fire or something like that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Around 4.00 or 5.00, I did hear some shooting, and this was a sign that something unusual was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please put your headphones on your ears, because in that case you will hear us better. Like that, yes. Thank you. Thank you. So please explain what happened. You spent a couple of days in your apartment, and then what happened?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Four or five days later, from the editor of the then radio station, Vaso Antic, I was informed by telephone that I needed to go to the radio station to act as a journalist, as a person who would keep the population informed, because I already had some experience as a stringer, especially specialising in sports reporting. So when I was called in, of course I responded, and from that day on, for the following year and a half, I worked as a reporter in the Samac radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And that was your work obligation, was it not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And you received a decision to that effect from the local defence ministry department, that that was your work obligation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Shortly after that, I received a decision that that was my work obligation, and like everyone else, I accepted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And when you went to the Radio Samac premises, what did you find there? What was the situation like? Who was there present? And what were you told regarding your future tasks under your work obligation duty?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Just as anyone else starting work somewhere, I was familiarised with the conditions of work. I found the editor, Vaso Antic, there; the sound engineer, or radio technician, whose name was Pasaga Tihic, who had also come there under the work obligation. In the studio there was the announcer, a lady - I don't remember her name now - and the other workers who were employed there. And then I was told by the editor what my tasks would be, and they were as follows --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down a little for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I was told that my tasks would be to inform the entire population about civilian life, to give them information that affected all civilians in the area; that I would also be going into the field, that I would be a reporter from the field; that I would truly and frankly keep the citizens of Samac and the surrounding villages informed regarding many matters of vital importance, and what was meant was distribution of food, distribution of humanitarian aid, the cases when there would be electricity cuts and water supply cuts and other matters of interest to the citizens; also other crucial issues in those days, and that was, despite the difficult conditions, the need to organise the education of children, vaccination of children; then also that I would have to go to various institutions, such as the health centre, the hospital. In other words, that I would simply inform the listeners of all matters of interest to the population on which their life depended. And these were the broad lines, but generally, it meant keeping them informed so that the population would feel well informed and protected and be able to continue living as best they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Did you also carry reports about developments on the front and the needs of the army?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In addition to the other duties I had was this one, to report from the front, because the relatives of the people in the military had a keen interest as to where they were, how they were doing, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I see. So you were a reporter. You mostly worked in the field, collecting information from the whole of the Samac municipality, what the needs of the population were, what could be done, what was the situation on the battlefield. Then you brought those reports to the offices and these were broadcast?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was my job. In those days, every inhabitant living in the territory of Samac municipality, be it in town or in the rural areas, couldn't wait to hear my voice with reports from the field, and the territory I covered was very large. Maybe I won't be exaggerating. But it covered an area of some 120 and 130 kilometres. It was a border region towards the neighbouring municipalities of Gradacac, Orasje, and Odzak, on the other side. Because Samac municipality had a quite specific geographic position.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please explain: What were people complaining of most? What kind of information did they give you when you interviewed them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: It was the kind of information that I would have given them if they had asked me, and that is the following: They were condemning everything that was going on at the time, because for many people this had caught them by surprise. Also, the difficulties that the people, the locals, the citizens, whatever you like to call them, were confronting, and there was a wide spectrum of difficulties that the people had to contend with, very difficult conditions of life. And of course, there was always a ray of hope that all this would blow over soon, and everyone said that they couldn't wait for it all to be over for them to go back to their normal life.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the kind of information you received from members of all nationalities?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of a journalist would I be if I were to provide information to one group and not to others? The information was addressed to all the population in town and in the villages and local communes of Samac municipality, and wherever, in fact, Radio Samac could be heard. So whatever I did, whatever I said, I did for the benefit of the entire population living there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you frequently visited the front lines, that you were in contact with the troops. Of what ethnicity were the army members?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I was in direct contact with all of them, so I'm well informed about that. Understandably, the largest group were Serbs, but there were also soldiers of other nationalities or ethnicities, both Muslims and Croats. I do not have the numbers, but I'm quite sure and I can claim that there were men of all ethnic groups who wanted to be where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cordasevic, tell us: Did you, during those first days, see anyone wearing white armbands, be they soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. This was at the very beginning. The first few days, these bands were worn - or ribbons - on the shoulder. These ribbons were worn by members of the army, that is, men in uniform. They were worn also by a certain number of civilians. I was one of them who had this ribbon on either one or other shoulder, depending on what the army determined. We wore these ribbons - and I am quite sure of that, because that is the reason why I wore it - so that people could tell that I belonged to the area, that I wasn't some outside element. Very briefly, it was a sign of identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Since the situation was difficult - the town was shelled frequently, there was a shortage of electricity and water - how did the population find food? Where did you have your meals?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: The greatest difficulties were, in fact, in the field of food, because that is one of the essential needs. The people did as best they could, but most of them fared like I did. There was a public canteen in the premises of Tekstilac plant. It was a public canteen where the troops were fed, as well as the civilian population. I went there too, and many of us ate there, and it was most welcome in those days. Whoever needed food would come to the canteen, so (canteen. )

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: So this means members of Croatian and Muslim ethnicity as well?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And in view of this very difficult situation with electricity, water, shelling, how did Radio Samac manage under those conditions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: It is not difficult to assume how it managed. In such circumstances, because of the aggravated situation, it was normal to expect that there were frequent interruptions in the airing of programmes. But we didn't just sit and wait, but we went on with our work, waiting for more favourable conditions. And these interruptions in broadcasts occurred primarily because of electricity cuts, then also because of certain other changes in the location of the radio. Then also, one must admit, the equipment was outdated, so there would be frequent failures, and sometimes, if we could get hold of a generator, they were not powerful enough. So that, in view of all these things, according to my assessment, I think that we were more off the air than on the air, and we were even criticised by the population for them not being able to hear us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell us whether there was a report aired on Radio Samac that Muslims and Croats had to wear white ribbons.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: You mean by the radio, on the radio. No. No. I never heard any such announcement. I never made such an announcement, nor did I ever hear about it, nor did I write such an announcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And was there a report announced on prohibiting more than three Muslims or Croats forming a group?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No. No such item was broadcast by the radio station in which I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And was any kind of report broadcast, or an order, for Muslims and Croats, any kind of order that would be discriminatory in relation to the population?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No, no such report was ever aired. We continued living together in Samac, all of us, those of us who wanted to stay on. We would meet and sit together and walk around together. So who would ever think of announcing any such thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In the period while you were a reporter working for Radio Samac in 1992 and 1993, did you receive any remuneration for your work?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I shared the fate of all others that had work obligation, which meant that I was happy to have the essentials I needed, that is, food. And under those difficult conditions, I did have some remuneration, which, true enough, was symbolic because of the devaluation of the currency in those days. I can't remember the exact amount - the value of the currency changed - but the amounts were minimal and very modest, but they were welcome. So I did receive remuneration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, tell us, please: In that period of time, who determined the editorial policies of the radio? And also, tell us at the same time who financed the work of Radio Samac.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that I was a reporter working in the field. The programme structure is normally up to the editor of the radio, and I was involved in implementing that programme schedule. As for the financing, since we belonged to the Secretariat for Social Affairs of the Municipal Assembly, then naturally, the finances came from them, in simplest terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The Secretariat for Social Affairs, was it under the Executive Council, that is, the government, or the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't have much contact with the secretariat. My duty was to do my part of the work properly. I just know that the Secretariat for Social Affairs is within the Municipal Assembly. Now, how it's regulated, probably the Executive Council is a higher-level body than the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did Mr. Blagoje Simic ever give you any orders as to what should be broadcast over the radio?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I, as a journalist, am concerned, no, because I had my own job description, and I've already told you what that was. I didn't make interviews of prominent figures. If that was necessary, someone else would do that. I was also just a journalist, and the editor is the editor, and he is the one who decides who would be interviewed and by whom. So I was not the person who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: But you were a journalist, a reporter. Do you have any knowledge as to certain people being detained in Samac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I do, and I do know that. I am aware of three locations in town where men were detained, probably because of investigations and interrogations. I don't know what exactly was being done there, but I do know that they existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about a tragic event that happened in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I heard of it. True, I learnt about it later, subsequent to the event itself. As this was the affair of the army, and as I was not engaged as a soldier, it is understandable that I didn't get any detailed information about it, but I heard about it, as did many other citizens living in the territory of the municipality. Samac is a small town, and reports spread very fast, even without the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a location called Zasavica, within Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's about six or seven kilometres from Samac. It's a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about who was living there in that period of time and what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I know that before the armed conflict, the village was mostly inhabited by Croats. I know that in this period of time, that there were also others living there in addition to Croats. There were Muslims and Croats, but also some Serbs who had come from some other areas. I know they lived there. I don't have a lot of information about it. The only thing I really do know, because this was of vital importance for all of us, was that there was a farm there where livestock was bred, and I know that this farm was the basis for the food that was provided in the public canteen where I had my meals. So it was a part of an agriculturalist state that existed there. That is as much as I know about Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Zasavica in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't in that period of time. I didn't have any need to go there. I had no relatives staying there for me to go and visit them. So I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, or had you heard rumours, that it was a kind of camp?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that there were any such rumours. I already said that it was inhabited by the people that I have described and that there was a farm there. I don't know anything about a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you joined the SDS after the outbreak of armed conflict. Tell me: In that period of time, that is, 1992 and 1993, did your party, at the local level, implement a policy of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Or a policy of discrimination, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Cross-examination for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Cordasevic, my name is David Re, a Prosecutor at The Hague. I'm going to ask you some questions about your testimony. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As journalist working both before and during the war, it was your job to be informed about what was going on, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: My job was to broadcast news about the civilian life, the life in the area, to transmit information which pertained to and affected all the population, which would benefit the entire population. I have already enumerated what my job -- the tasks contained within my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When giving your answers, could I ask you, please, to be as brief as possible and to respond to the question I ask, and not answer another one. As a journalist, you have to be informed to broadcast the information, don't you? It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: So within the ambit of the work which I did --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You have to gather information, don't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I went to different institutions. I went to basements, shelters, public canteens, to the front line. I talked to people in the streets, I went to schools, to establishments, to all places where I could gather information which would be of interest and benefit to the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course. You wouldn't be doing your job as a journalist otherwise, would you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And of course, as a journalist, you also make contacts or use contacts? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the civilian population, as well as with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In your job -- you told us earlier your job was to provide information over Radio Samac about what was happening in the war and in the town. Your contacts -- you would have needed contacts with the government, the military, and the police?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, to a lesser extent with them, because this was up to the editor and not up to me, because I was a field reporter, and I reported from the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Journalists, Mr. Cordasevic, prize their contacts, don't they, the people who provide them with information on matters about which they're reporting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Because these contacts can give you valuable information which you can use to report, or can give you leads; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In your job in reporting from the front line, you had contacts with members of the military, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You relied upon those people to give you information?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have contacts in the 2nd Posavina Brigade command? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who were your main military contacts during 1992 and 1993? Just the names, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I had none. I didn't have any contacts of that kind. I was a journalist in the field, putting together programmes aimed at informing the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just please stick to the point. I'm asking you about your contacts in the military. You've already told us you needed contacts to obtain information to compile your reports. You must have got the information from people in the military. Who were the people in the military - just their names, please - who were your main sources of information during 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I just had talks with soldiers on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Including, of course, officers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: The commanding officers were with their troops. The petty [phoen] officers were with their troops on the front line then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You also broadcast information about what was -- about civilian activities, and to do so, you would have needed to obtain accurate information from the civilian authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No. This is also up to the editor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you had worked as a psychologist in Samac before the war. Did I hear that correctly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Pedagogist and psychologist. That's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Blagoje Simic was a medical practitioner in the town. Did you have professional contacts with him as another -- as a health professional working in the same area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you know him quite well?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, to the extent which was necessary, because, after all, he was a doctor and we worked together in a humanitarian association. It was an association to control, to combat, alcoholism and drug addiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You weren't the only announcer working at the radio station, were you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You didn't listen to Radio Samac all the time when it was broadcasting, did you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't have occasion -- much occasion for that, because I was in the field most of the time preparing my material for the programme, for the broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So, of course, you can't tell us what was broadcast about anything when you were in the field gathering your reports, because you didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You know Simeon Simic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Bozo Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The radio station was socially owned during the war, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Yes, by -- it was a fixed asset of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the director of the radio station was appointed by the Municipal Assembly, or the Executive Board or Council of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in the war, war period, that was -- the function of the Municipal Assembly was taken by the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: This social affairs department was within the framework of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly was replaced by the -- its functions were carried out by the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency during the war, 1992 and 1993, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And they -- and you, of course, knew that Blagoje Simic was president of the Crisis Staff, didn't you, and War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who were the other members of the Crisis Staff? Was Milan Simic on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who was on the Crisis Staff or in the War Presidency. I repeat: I did my work in the field. I was not interested in that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were able to leave Samac and return to Samac for the purposes of your war reporting, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were able to leave freely and return freely, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I had a pass issued to me by the army. I also had a sticker on my car. And of course, I was subject to check-ups wherever I went, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you work at the radio station before the war, that's before April 17th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: From 1970, from the beginning of that radio, but only in the sports programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There were Croat and Muslim employees of Radio Samac, or Bosanski Samac, before the war, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: After April 17th, 1992, the municipality of Samac came under Serb control, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The radio station was then -- from then on was under Serb management, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how that segment was organised, but it was in the service of the people who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff and War Presidency were a Serb Crisis Staff and Serb War Presidency, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And as the highest civilian officials or authority in Samac during the war, they ultimately controlled the radio station, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: We were within the framework of the civilian authorities of the Municipal Assembly, that is, civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which were Serb controlled; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is true that the majority of the people who remained there were Serbs, but also others remained there, of the other ethnicities, and they all listened to the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there any Croat or Muslim announcers on Radio Samac after the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No. Well, initially, yes, but later, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How much later? Are we talking days here, days after the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps two or three months. There was a technician working, as part of his work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The only non-Serb employee was this technician after that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Serb forces, in fact, seized control of the radio station on about the 17th of April, 1992, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the radio station was guarded by soldiers, wasn't it, or armed police?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I saw a soldier, soldiers, but whether it was guarded, and in which way it was guarded, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There were armed people outside the radio station to prevent unauthorised people from gaining entry, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, control and check-ups had been intensified at all points, which was only logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the radio station. The answer to my question was yes, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: There was heightened security all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the radio station. There were armed people outside the radio station stopping unauthorised people gaining entry, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, heightened control there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the editor, was he a member of the SDS as well? That's Vaso Antic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were the other announcers SDS members?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: You might find it hard to believe, but that is something I wasn't interested in at all. I just went about doing my job properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you answer my question? Were they SDS members or not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: They were probably sympathisers. I don't know who were actual members. I was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Radio Samac broadcast local government or local civilian announcements, didn't it, announcements of the Crisis Staff, War Presidency, and Executive Board, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know much about that. I worked in the field gathering what was within the purview of my job. As to different announcements and warnings, and if those were of vital importance, this was not something which was within my ambit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you involved in the broadcasting or the announcement of the declaration of the state of emergency over Radio Samac after the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No. That is also up to the editor and for the announcer to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Because that was certainly broadcast over Radio Samac, wasn't it, the declaration of the state of emergency in Samac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it had to be within the context of the worsened situation that attained, but I had no occasion to hear it in detail or in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Radio Samac broadcast to the citizens of Samac that Serb forces had taken control of Radio Samac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How often did Simeon Simic visit Radio Samac when you were there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps -- well, I worked with him for only a couple of months, and I only saw him two or three times. Mine was to work in the field, and his was to work at the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: One of the functions of Radio Samac during the war was to boost the morale of the civilian population, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And it did that by giving them information and entertaining them, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It played music too, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was welcome, in the circumstances, everything which was popular before and during the war, and they had music at all these stations with that view in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It played Serb patriotic songs, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, occasionally, those too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It didn't play Croat patriotic songs, did it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, much less, much less or never, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think "never" is the right answer, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I can't claim that, because I didn't listen much to the radio. I didn't have much chance to listen to the radio. I can't claim that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You never heard Radio Samac play Croat patriotic songs after the ... END OF RECORDING.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It played what could be called Chetnik songs, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You never heard Chetnik songs being played?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, patriotic songs from time to time, but there was also other kind of music which did not -- not necessarily of an ethnic character. There were just nice songs, all sorts of nice music.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... for interrupting. Maybe my learned friend can give a few examples, because it's rather, you know, maybe a matter of interpretation. For one it's a patriotic song, for the other it's a folk song or -- you know. So maybe my learned friend can -- if we have some names of these songs, maybe he can ask this witness and then he can get -- obtain the answer. Thank you. PRESIDING OFFICER: So, Mr. Pantelic, you're seeking a clarification; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: A clarification, yes, Madam Presiding Officer. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And could I have a minute out for that very detailed clarification, please, Madam Presiding Officer? PRESIDING OFFICER: Yes, and you have 17 minutes on your bank account of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Presiding Officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Cordasevic, was "From Topola to Ravna Gora," what that one of the songs that you heard played on the radio, "From Topola to Ravna Gora"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: It's hard to remember whether I heard that particular song.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about "General Drazic's Troops Are Everywhere"? Was that one of the songs that you heard played on Radio Samac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall now what songs I listened to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's quite possible that those were the types of songs that were played; you would agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Patriotic songs were played occasionally; I will agree with that. Now, as to playing Chetnik and nationalistic songs, I didn't hear those.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And Stevan Todorovic used to come into the radio station, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I spent the least of my time at the radio station. Perhaps I can remember one or two of his visits. Others would be able to tell you more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But you certainly heard -- you saw him there a couple of times, but you heard that he used to come in quite regularly, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear that he used to come regularly. The journalist did not inform me about visits and the frequency of visits of other people. I wasn't important enough for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Simo Zaric came to the radio station, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't that. I didn't see him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Todorovic would come and order the radio station staff to play Chetnik songs, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection. Calling for speculation. Maybe the question could be rephrased. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't intend to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The question was: Stevan Todorovic used to come to the radio station and order the staff to play Chetnik songs, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You went to the municipal building to meet Blagoje Simic during 1992 and 1993, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I had no reason to go. It was up to the editor to talk to others. My job was to work on the ground with civilian population, because I knew the area well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your job, you said in your evidence earlier to Mr. Vukovic, was to truly and frankly keep the citizens of Samac informed.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: About the material that I had prepared, and pursuant to the information that was available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Radio Samac could be heard by troops on the front line, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: It most of the areas, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You've already agreed that one of the things that Radio Samac was doing -- or one of its roles was to keep -- was to boost civilian morale. It also attempted to boost military morale too, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: It's hard to distinguish; therefore, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The enemy you were fighting, that is, the Serb forces were fighting at the time, were Croats and Muslims, weren't they? You would know that from your job on the front line.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And information was broadcast over Radio Samac, intended to demoralise the enemy, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Partially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And Radio Samac reported on war crimes against Serb forces and civilians, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't quite get your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Radio Samac reported on war crimes committed by Croat and Muslim forces against Serb forces and Serb civilians, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: There were cases of that too, within the scope of what was available.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Radio Samac reported on those things, didn't it, broadcast it; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: To the extent that it was available, that there was information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Radio Samac also reported on genocide against the Serbian people, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Radio Samac didn't report on alleged war crimes committed by Serb troops or civilians against Croats or Muslims, did it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When Radio Samac was referring to the Croats, it referred to them as the Ustasha forces, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: During that critical period of time, all of the media used occasionally those terms, as it Radio Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When referring to the forces of the Bosnian government, the central government, it referred to -- it called them the Muslim forces or the Muslim army, didn't it? That's Radio Samac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It referred to the Bosnian government as Muslim extremists, and their army as Muslim extremists, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: There were certainly cases of that as well too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In your job of truly and frankly keeping the citizens of Samac informed, did Radio Samac report on the detention of hundreds of non-Croat - sorry - non-Serbs in the facilities, the four facilities around the town? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did it -- did Radio Samac report on the isolation of Croats in Zasavica in its job of keeping the citizens --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did it report on bribes being paid to officials to allow people to be exchanged from Samac to other places?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In keeping the citizens of Samac truly and frankly informed, did it report upon the beating and torture of detainees in the SUP, MUP, primary and elementary schools?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did it report upon the massacre of 16 Croats by Serb paramilitaries in May 1992 at Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did it report, in its reports on the work obligation, on civilians, non-Serb civilians, being forced to dig trenches at the front lines while under enemy fire?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did it report upon the looting of non-Serb property by non-Serbo-Croats and Muslims who were forced to do so by Serb --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- armed guards? The answer is no?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did it report upon the isolation of Croats or the order of the Crisis Staff ordering Croats to be isolated and taken to vital facilities in the town?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Those things would have been of interest to the Croats and Muslims in town, who were part of your audience, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: The programme of the department for information is something that is decided upon by the editor, not a person reporting from the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The mass arrest of non-Serbs only because they were non-Serbs; their isolation, their detention, beating, torture, only because they were non-Serbs; the taking of their houses because they were non-Serbs; the looting of their property because they were non-Serbs; and the deportation from Samac because they were non-Serbs, would amount to ethnic cleansing, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I was not involved in the political aspect of it. You can put questions to me that have to do with my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Vukovic about SDS local policies. I just put a number of things to you in relation to ethnic cleansing. The things I put to you, you have to agree, would amount to ethnic cleansing, wouldn't they? I can list them again if you like.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the fact that the SDS participated in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was asking you if those things - the mass arrest of non-Serbs because they were non-Serbs, their detention because they were non-Serbs, their torture, their beating, because they were non-Serbs, the isolation of Croats because they were not Serbs, the taking of their houses because they were not Serbs, the expulsion of these people from Bosanski Samac because they weren't Serbs - that would amount to ethnic cleansing, wouldn't it, and you, as a psychologist and educated man, would have to agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection. Calling for speculation. This is a legal matter. This is a legal issue, and this witness is not a legal professional, so I don't know how he can answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I press the question on the basis "ethnic cleansing" isn't a legal term, and it was put to the witness by the counsel who called him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Again I ask the question: All those things would amount to ethnic cleansing, as you understand the term, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Everything you listed would amount to bad things. Now, as to where exactly it happened, what happened, I had no information concerning that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were asked about ethnic cleansing by Mr. Vukovic. I'm asking you, simply: The things I've just listed, you can agree, would amount to ethnic cleansing if they occurred? Yes or no. I'm not asking you whether they occurred; I'm just asking you whether, if they did occur, they would amount to ethnic cleansing, in the commonly understood definition of the term. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I never studied the definition of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sir, you, of course, joined the SDS because you agreed with its policies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I agreed with their policies, yes, I did. How else would I become their member?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You, of course, agreed with its leadership as well, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Not always, but in the majority of cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: One of its published policies in May 1992 was to establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities. The leaders of the SDS - Krajisnik, Plavsic, and Karadzic - have been indicted for persecution. You understand and you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I know that they had been indicted, but I don't know the details of it. That is too political for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic has pleaded guilty to persecuting non-Serbs throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, and one of the things she has agreed with SDS policy, which amounted to persecution, was establishing state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities. You're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I'm only aware of the plea agreement of Mrs. Plavsic, but I have no clue as to the details of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: One of the Serb -- one of the SDS policies was to "establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities," published on the 12th of -- promulgated by the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 12th of May, 1992. That was the policy of the party you joined in 1992.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that particular conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You have remained in the party, despite the indictment of its three leaders for persecution and crimes against humanity, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I remained in the party, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You remained in the party even after the massacre of thousands of Muslim men in Srebrenica in 1995, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat again that I am a member of the party, yes. Now, as to the details, I don't know much about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You remained in the party despite its carrying out of ethnic cleansing and persecution of non-Serbs across the Republika Srpska, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the ethnic cleansing committed by this party. Nobody discussed that in my presence, nor was I asked to participate in ethnic cleansing, nor did my party participate in ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So you're seriously telling the Trial Chamber that, as a journalist, you are unaware of ethnic cleansing committed by the SDS leadership or the VRS? Is that your serious evidence here?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, do you know: After the breakout of hostilities, when was the first session of the Municipal Assembly of Samac held following that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you whether you knew -- or rather, whether it was announced on the radio that non-Serbs were leaving Samac. Do you know the reasons for certain non-Serb families to leave Samac, not only after the breakout of the war but also before that and during it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I know that some people were leaving town due to specific geographical location of the place itself. All of those who believed they would be better off in town remained, and all of those who believed that they would be better off leaving left from the area where there was fighting going on. It is true that there were more Croats and Muslims leaving, but there was also a significant number of Serbs that left.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And did a certain number of non-Serbs remain there during the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and nobody knows that better than me, because they remained living there with us, working with us, and there were Muslims in some associations, in some clubs. There were Muslims playing in the football club Borac during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
