utterances.text: You said to the Prosecutor, when asked about the programme that was aired, you said that there had been certain warnings announced.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of warnings were those?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Warnings, announcements to the residents concerning power outages, water outages, vaccinations, school enrollment for children, distribution of food to the population, warnings about possible shellings, going to shelters, all of those things that residents were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please tell us: How long did you remain as a journalist in Radio Samac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Until 1993, basically for a year and a half, and then I went on to another job.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: When was Mr. Simo Simic appointed director of Radio Samac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was just prior to my departure from the radio station, some three months before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: So in 1993?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, thereabouts, towards the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you this as well: The warnings that you have just mentioned, did they pertain to all of the residents?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: I've already said so several times. They pertain to all of the residents, because they were of interest to all of the people living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Regardless of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Ethnicity is of no consequence here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the vicinity of Samac, or rather, across from it, is Slavonski Samac, even nowadays. Were you able to listen to Croatian radio station?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one could listen to them, but I don't know whether it was Djakovo or Osijek radio stations. It might have been even Orasje radio stations. Yes, from the neighbouring areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And did you hear some Serbian songs played on those Croatian radio stations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us about their vocabulary, what terms they used referring to Serbs?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: We adopted from them some of our terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us what kind of terminology.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: To call the opposing side the enemy side. They referred to us as Chetniks. Those are the terms they used, nationalistically coloured, and they used such terms as "Muslims," "balijas," "Ustashas," and so on. But, rather, we used these terms much less frequently than they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Are you aware of the fact that Croats and Muslims were sequestered in Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that, but I know that there were different kinds of people living there. However, they had not been isolated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I have just one further question for you. Do you know or do you have any information that there had been a decision of the Crisis Staff concerning isolation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there had been any kind of order on forcing out non-Serb population from Samac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was an order on imprisoning non-Serbs, on torturing them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR CORDASEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. I believe that there was no such decision; however, I was only concerned with doing my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you, Mr. Cordasevic, for coming here today to give your deposition. It's concluded now and you can go. Thank you. Ten minutes' break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 11.12 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Good morning, Mr. Savic. Could you please stand and read the solemn declaration in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. PRESIDING OFFICER: You may sit down. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. For the record, please tell us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: My name is Milos Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Mrki.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, you will be explaining that later on, but since you are a very seriously war-disabled person, to the extent of 90 per cent disabled, should, at any point in time during your testimony, should you not feel well or need a break, please feel free to ask for one. We won't hurry. We'll adjust to your physical abilities. So please feel quite at ease, and if at any point in time you feel you're unwell, please let us know, and Madam Presiding Officer will take care of it. When were you born, Mr. Savic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 9th of January, 1957.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: In the village of Gajevi.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Where are you residing now?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: In Bajevo [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: In Gajevi. I'm currently living in Gajevi.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your current occupation is a farmer, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm working on my own land. I'm tilling my own land.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But you have a secondary-school degree and you are a mechanic by occupation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You did your national military service when?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what branch of the army did you serve in?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: In a motorised unit. I was a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Up until 1990, you were not politically active?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in 1990, you became a member of which party?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you still a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Will you please explain whether, at the end of 1991, you received a call-up paper, that is, whether you were mobilised to units of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: At the end of October/beginning of November 1991, I was called up by the Territorial Defence of Samac and I was mobilised to a company in the village, in the village I lived in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your village unit belonged to which larger unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: It was part of the 1st Detachment of the Tactical Group 17, Pelagicevo, under the command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Savic: What was your duty in the 1st Detachment when you were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I was a courier in my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Describe for us briefly what your military engagement in that period meant, what kind of military duties you had during the day, whether you were accommodated in a barracks or in a camp, or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: In those days, I stayed on in my own house. During the day, the commanders would call if there was any need to distribute call-up papers, to tell people to come to a meeting, to be familiarised with weapons, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Savic: The other members of the 1st Detachment from your village had also been mobilised, like you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The whole village had been mobilised. Everyone had received call-up papers, and more or less everyone had responded to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But your village and the environs, how would you describe it ethnically? Was it a mixed community or a Serb-dominated community?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: My village is a Serb village. There were only some five or six Muslim households in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Within the 1st Detachment, of which you were a member, were there members of other nationalities in addition to Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What nationalities were they?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Muslims, and I think there were some Croats as well. I know those people from the street, but it's difficult to tell all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you were mostly at home, and if need be, you performed these military duties as a kind of reserve force?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. All I did was what I did at home. I farmed the land, I looked after the livestock, and I did this courier work when necessary, and in the evening I worked in a restaurant called Zvijezda, as a waiter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly explain for us the atmosphere in the territory of Samac municipality, and of course in your village itself and around it, regarding interethnic relations in the period from January 1992 to April 1992. What are your personal impressions and memories of that period?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the situation was rather tense there was a lot of coming and going through the villages, there were barricades in some villages that we didn't go into much, but we had reliable information about them. We were -- this psychosis had spread from Croatia, so that over here where we were, we expected something like that to happen too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, when we discussed your testimony in these proceedings, you mentioned that towards the end of March 1992 you went to attend a course, some kind of military training in handling certain weapons and so on.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell us a little about that, how it came about that you went to this course, upon whose orders, where it was held, and how long it lasted, and what you were taught. You tell us in your own words, and if necessary, I will put some additional questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of March, a report arrived to my company, from the battalion, that our company - that is, four younger men, who were ready and willing to learn about weapons - should go, and the deputy company commander -- actually, in the company, they agreed, pursuant to the orders of the 1st Battalion of the 17th Tactical Group, who the four men would be, and the company commander read out those four names. I was among them. Savic Milos, Lukic Petar, Lukic Cedo [phoen], and Duzic Zeljko [phoen]. And from the village of Gajevo, we went in a private vehicle to Batkusa, and then, with the others, we moved on. There were about 15 to 18 of us. We didn't know exactly where we were going, but knowing the surroundings, I realised we were close to Ilok. We were travelling in civilian clothes, without weapons, because around Orasje and Brcko there were barricades, searches of passengers, and to facilitate our trip, we travelled as civilians. We got to somewhere close to Ilok, to a camp there. We found a group of inspectors there, people we hadn't known. They were wearing camouflage uniforms and they addressed us officially. They never mentioned any names, only nicknames, and I don't even remember those nicknames now. They called each other by nickname. And when we arrived there, they told us that the training would be quite strenuous, a lot of physical, hard work, physical fitness training, that we would be some sort of an intervention unit. We didn't really know what that meant. We stayed there 12 to 15 days, then we returned home. We had learnt as much as we could regarding the handling of those rifles, hand-held rocket launchers, grenades, and suchlike.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. If I am right, you must have returned to your unit, that is, the 1st Detachment, if my calculations are right, around perhaps the 13th or 14th of April, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. I think it was around the 12th. I never took note of those dates anywhere, but it was thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you returned, what kind of military assignment did you have?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Of course, when we returned, we went back to our detachment and we tried to pass on some of the knowledge we had been taught by our instructors to our friends and comrades in the village. That was our job.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Savic, whether you are aware of the arrival of a group from Serbia, around about that time, in the territory of Samac. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any direct knowledge. I heard from others that a group of some 30 guys had arrived. We didn't know who they were or what they were, but we heard that they had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What do you know about them? Were they independent in their activities or did they come under the control of a unit or a command?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: They were independent of us, but they were under the command of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Savic: In your unit, and on the basis of your personal knowledge at that time, was there an information about the military situation in the Samac area? Because, after all, you were a military man at the time. You ... END OF RECORDING ... at that time you were a soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the situation was rather tense. There was some information, either through intelligence people or informers. We were told that an action was being prepared on the other side of the Sava River from Prud, which was inhabited mostly by Croats. And during our training period, there had been barricades, and it had not been possible to enter or leave Samac. And as far as I was informed, apparently this had been done, these barricades had been erected by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Will you please describe to us now, to the best of your recollection: What did you, as a soldier, as a member of the 1st Detachment, do, or rather, what were your assignments and duties in the night between the 16th and 17th of April, 1992? Slowly and clearly, from beginning to end.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, I was in the village, in my own village, at home, when a courier arrived from Batkusa, where the command of the 1st Detachment was. He came to tell me that we should go to Batkusa immediately. It was late afternoon/early evening. We went there. That is where the command was. We spent an hour, two or three there, and then we were told that we had to go to Samac, that is, a group of us who had undergone training, that we should go to Samac to assist in protecting the silos where food was stored, the wheat, the grain was stored.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who told you that, that you should go there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: The commander, and he received orders from his superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now tell me: Around what time was this that you went to the silo in Samac, to that position?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: We went to that position at the silo just before midnight, I think. I think it was before midnight. And when we arrived there, we found men from the 4th Detachment who were already there. So we climbed onto the silo, which is about 20 or 30 metres high, and we took our positions there. And then our commander, Aco Jankovic, was in communication, and we heard that their communications were operating. Now, whether he intercepted that communication or not, I don't know. But anyway, he told us that they were not allowing any civilian vehicles from Babina Greda or Sikirevci to move towards the Samac bridge. And around 2.00 a.m., we were able to see a large line of headlights moving towards the Samac bridge. These were not civilian vehicles; these were ATCs or tanks. They made a lot of noise. Ordinary vehicles would not make such a noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And where was this coming from?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: It was coming from the Croatian side. We couldn't see the vehicles, but we could see their lights, because it was night-time, and we were positioned high up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And around what time -- did an armed operation begin, and around what time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: What happened was that they opened fire at us at the silo. Shells hit the silo where I was, and in town there was a bit of shooting from infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Madam Presiding Officer, this witness -- according to the summary, Mr. Savic was born on January 9th, 1959 -- and you can remove this time that I'm speaking from your time of direct examination. I have no objection to that. He now lives in Samac. He was a member of the reserve JNA unit in 1992. He attended the military course in the village near Ilok, and afterwards he joined the special battalion in Samac. He will testify on the following facts and events related to the defendant: The defendant was not in charge of recruiting volunteers for special training, and defendant never organised such activity. Half of his -- more than half; three quarters of his testimony has been outside of this summary. 1) We have not received any proper discovery or notice of any of this man's testimony so far today; and 2) it's totally outside the scope of the summary that was provided to us. I have allowed him to go on a bit. I've given them some latitude. But now this is well beyond any type of notice that we've been provided. This is another notice violation and discovery violation on behalf of the defendant Blagoje Simic, and I want the record to note that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe that's the position of the Prosecution, but the interpretation of the Defence is very simple. We are speaking about the personal involvement of this witness in the training outside of territory of Samac, then his membership in a special battalion, and inevitably, all events when he was a member of the special battalion, including the night of 16th to 17th of April. So everything is linked and connected to his personal involvement and his personal knowledge. And I think that this objection from the Prosecution side is unfounded, and I will proceed, and I will leave to Trial Chamber to finally decide about the objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I understand that, and it would be very nice if you gave us notice. You list one particular event that this person is going to testify to. The rest of it, we've had no notice of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Here it is. Do you want to read it? Do you want to read it for the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but in fact it is not in dispute that there was an armed conflict on the night of 16th or 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's not in dispute; however, there was a conflict --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's a well-known fact in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: However, if you want to discuss it, you have to list it in your summary, to give proper notice for the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's a background of the events where this witness was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's a summary of the facts, and we've had no notice of these facts. That's for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We don't have to put any kind of -- you have that in your indictment, all these facts, so that's very simple. We are speaking about the indictment. PRESIDING OFFICER: You can proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I kindly ask to have additional five minutes because of this -- PRESIDING OFFICER: It's not five minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Give me three -- give me three -- PRESIDING OFFICER: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. PRESIDING OFFICER: Three. Three. It's three minutes, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I ask more to get what -- PRESIDING OFFICER: Yeah, yeah, sure. It's three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Savic, please describe, in brief: When you were on top of the silo, what -- how did this military operation go? What happened? Did anyone shoot at the silo, or what?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: A shell was fired from the Croatian side at the silo and hit the silo, on which I was. And also in town we could hear some skirmishes, some shooting. Whether these were smaller groups or not, we couldn't tell, because it was night and we couldn't see, in fact, and we had no reports coming from town at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you this, because in some of the notes which I jotted down when we talked, when I talked to you, perhaps you recollected some things wrong. You said that when your detachment came and was assigned to the silo, that you met members of the 4th Detachment. Do you still stick to this, or was it perhaps something else?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I think they were members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you impeaching your own witness, Counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm just -- there was a problem with the interpretation. I mean, not from interpreters' booth; it's a problem with his explanation of that. So I just tried to clarify that. Because he mentioned 1st Detachment and then the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, Mr. Savic. What happened at dawn on April 17th?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: At dawn on the 17th of April, there were JNA units in town who were, in fact, our lads who had been mobilised, who had been called up. They moved around town disarming these smaller groups and manning all the vital facilities in town, and this was the information that was available to us up there on the silo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And where was your group at dawn on the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Our group remained on the silo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you spent the whole day on the 17th of April on the silo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were there all day on the silo. All the reports or the information that we received, what we could hear, was -- what I could hear when I went to the artesian well to fetch water in town, when I heard that they were handing over their weapons there, that people were bringing their weapons and surrendering them over at the police station. This I heard from people I know, from people I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Another question regarding this group which went for training: Were members of this group elected on the basis of party affiliation or was this strictly a matter of military categorisation or military principle?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: This group which went there for training was there on a purely military principle basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what happened afterwards? Where were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I was wounded on the 25th of May, 1992. We spent some time there upon the silo, and we spent the time until I was wounded, or rather, we were there three or four days; and from there, we went to a part of Grebnice. Our unit was standing by there in order to intervene in case of any casualties which needed to be pulled out, the dead, wounded needed to be pulled out, so that we were there in the Grebnice and Novo Selo, Samac area, and Obudovac and that area, generally, with that task. So we stayed there for two to three days and were transferred to the centre of Obudovac from there. There, an intervention unit was established consisting of young men, mostly lads from the unit in which I had been trained. We were there, and the military police. Also was there from these companies, i.e. battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Did Dr. Blagoje Simic play any role whatsoever in sending you personally to that training?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection. This is direct examination. This is not cross-examination. You can't ask leading questions like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Savic: What is your personal knowledge as regards Blagoje Simic, in connection with the training that you underwent? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: My personal knowledge -- to my personal knowledge, Blagoje Simic and the SDS had nothing to do with the sending of these lads to that particular training course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to the other young men who underwent this training? Did you ask them about the phases on which they had been sent there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not -- I hadn't known all these guys before we arrived at this camp. There, of course, we met, because we worked together, we were accommodated together. And as we had not much contact with the instructor other than during the training, we talked among each other. So they told me that they had been summoned for training within the framework of a call-up. You couldn't very well refuse a military summons at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did any one of these people who were with you mention Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: No, no one made any reference to Blagoje Simic, or mentioned anyone else, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in the end, Mr. Savic, please tell us, because you yourself were severely wounded and spent a long period in hospital with treatment and recovery: How many of your friends got wounded or killed during these military operations at the Samac front line? Do you have an approximate number?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the period which I spent there, until the 25th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No. Generally, if you know.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I know that it is a large number, but I don't know what number it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And until the time of your wounding, do you know how many people had been wounded or killed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that we went there to pull out the dead and the wounded, but as to the exact number, I don't know. I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is quite okay. Thank you. PRESIDING OFFICER: Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Savic. My name is Phillip Weiner. I'm with the Office of the Prosecutor, and I'm going to ask you some questions over the next 25 minutes. Okay? Do you understand that? Okay. Sir, let's talk about the selection process of the soldiers, like yourself, for training. You were not in charge of that training, first; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I have not understood the question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were not in charge of the training in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were not involved in selecting any of the persons to be trained?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were not involved in making recommendations of the persons to be trained?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I was not involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Basically, you had no responsibilities in the decision-making process as to those persons who would be trained? You were just a trainee. You had no decision-making -- you weren't involved in the decision-making process of who would be sent to training. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had nothing to do with that. I went there with these other lads on orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated you were a member of the SDS. Did you know the defendant Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I did not know Blagoje Simic before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you knew he was a leader in the SDS, local SDS leader?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I had heard this from people, because people said that he was the elected president.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, having not known him at the time, you weren't present with Dr. Simic in any meetings that he was involved in?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I was not at a single meeting, because I was not politically affiliated. I was just a plain party member.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You weren't present with Dr. Simic in any meetings where there were discussions about potential trainees; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I did not attend a single meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You weren't present with Dr. Simic during any conversations that he had with others, be it political leaders or military, concerning the training programme or the selection of trainees; you weren't present for any of those types of meetings or conversations?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I told you that I was not politically active. I was just in my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question is, if you listen to my question carefully: You weren't present when Dr. Simic had any conversations with anyone else, whether it's military personnel or political leaders, concerning that training or the selection of trainees; you weren't present for any of those conversations. Isn't that correct? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection. This is --

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- misleading question, and this witness is trying to be confused, because certain assumptions that Blagoje Simic was at certain meetings with certain people in order to make this kind of mobilisation is absolutely unfounded. So maybe you could rephrase your question in order not to mislead this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There's no misleading of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The question is: Were you present for any conversations Blagoje Simic had relating to the training or trainees -- or the selection of trainees? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And obviously, you were never present for any telephone calls Blagoje Simic made relating to the training or trainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection. Calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Whether he was present or not is not speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The question is: Were you present --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The speculation is whether Mr. Blagoje Simic was speaking about that or calling someone with that regard. That's speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you present, sir, for any telephone calls which Blagoje Simic made relating to the training or the selection of trainees? Were you present while he made any telephone calls in relation to that subject?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't present, because I had no opportunity to be near him at all, and I don't think that he had anything to do with the assignment of that group for training.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you present during conversations between Blagoje Simic and SDS officials? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection. On which occasion? Which period? With -- who was present there? What -- it's absolutely irrelevant question. You have to be more specific. What is the personal knowledge of this witness of such-and-such meeting where these people were present, at which time, et cetera. Otherwise, it's absolutely irrelevant

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you present, prior to the notice of training, for any meetings between -- or meetings or conversations between Dr. Blagoje Simic and SDS officials?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I was not present at any consultation meeting, at any meeting of any kind, because I was in my village. I didn't even know Blagoje Simic. I only met him after I had been wounded and after I returned from hospital and the recovery at hospital. The only thing which I had heard was that I had heard that this man was the president of the SDA [sic]. I didn't know him at all. We live several -- or were some several kilometres away. He did his job at a school and I was doing mine. I had no occasion to meet him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You said in your testimony a second ago - and I think it's a mistake, and I just want to clarify the record - you said president of the SDA. Do you mean president of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: My mistake. Sorry. SDS. SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, one last question on this same subject. You were never present for any conversation or meeting between Dr. Blagoje Simic and any military officials? And once again, this is prior to your receiving notice. You weren't present for any of that; correct? You were not; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you went for training in Ilok? Am I pronouncing that right: Ilok? And where is that located? Is that in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: In Croatia. It's more or less at the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who conducted this training?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: The training was conducted by some instructors, by men, members of special units, in camouflage uniforms, men whom we didn't know, and we couldn't learn what unit was actually involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's continue on units. You indicated you were a member of the 1st Detachment. You were aware that there were four detachments until the area; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: These four detachments were part of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Stevan Nikolic was the commander of that group?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And there were other units in that group, including a tank or APC unit from Brcko, a small tank or APC unit, and various other units in that group; correct? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you heard that there were volunteers from Serbia which came and was added to that 17th Tactical Group, the volunteers from Serbia came, about April 11th or so?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you aware that they arrived in Batkusa?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I heard in the village that they had arrived, some sort of a group of about 30-odd people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you aware that they had arrived by JNA helicopters?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I didn't -- I wasn't aware, but I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And had you also heard that they were met by JNA personnel and that Colonel Nikolic saw to it that they were given housing, food, transportation? Were you aware of that or did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you didn't know where they were staying or who was providing for their food or housing or any of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know. We didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you talk about these Serb volunteers, you're talking about the ones Crni, Debeli, Lugar, that group of Serb volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that this is the group that I later heard among whom were men with these nicknames that you are now mentioning, but whose volunteers these were, I don't know. I know that they were there and that they were under the command of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And they were brought in to assist the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, they didn't come in to fight the 17th Tactical Group; they came in to be part of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is probably so, but I had nothing to do with it. I was not there in the command. This was not information that I was privy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the 17th Tactical Group was involved, as you testified, in war operations or military operations early morning hours April 16th, April 17th, April 18th and 19th, is that correct, including the detachments, these special groups, involved in military operations during those days; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: The 17th Tactical Group was the command, and they did the commanding. It was at their orders that I went to the silo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And your small group wasn't the only group that was out there; there were other groups that apparently had been ordered out, because you saw 4th Detachment people. There were other groups of people from the 17th Command [sic] also out there during the 16th, 17th, and 18th and 19th?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you see these camouflage people, while you were up in these silos, moving around, the 16th, 17th, 18th? Does it come -- these camouflage people, did they come from Serbia, moving around the city, during those days?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to these camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Like the Serbs from Serbia were wearing, that special group with the camouflage uniforms, did you see them moving through the city from -- that were part of the 17th Tactical Group, on the 16th, 17th, 18th, and 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that the various groups within the 17th Tactical Unit were coordinating their activities? Such as your group, the 1st Detachment, was up in the silos; another group was guarding the bridge; another group was on the waterfront. So the various units were being coordinated by the commanders. Or you were told what to do by your commander --

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: -- and you relieved the 4th Detachment that was at the silo, or did you work together with them at the silo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I think that we were together, as far as I can recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So your commander sent you to the silo. So the 1st Detachment -- members of the 1st Detachment were sent to the silo, and whoever was in command of the 4th Detachment sent some of their people to the silo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, because I saw them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And obviously, you have to do what your commanders tell you to do.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And as you know, in the JNA army, there's a chain of command, or there was at that time -- while the JNA was in Bosnia, there was a chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you had Colonel Nikolic, of the 17th Tactical Group, in charge. He had -- correct? Colonel Nikolic was in charge of the 17th Tactical Group and he gave orders downward and eventually got to the soldiers, like yourself, and you were told what to do; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you couldn't just disobey the orders of the commander; you did what you were told to do, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And even the group that came in from Serbia was part of the 17th Tactical Group, which answered to Colonel Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were -- yes, they were there under that command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then eventually the military unit changed because the JNA was ordered out, in May, and the army of the Republika Srpska was established; isn't that correct? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And those groups that were part of the 17th Tactical Group became part of the 2nd Posavina Brigade -- I'm sorry. 2nd Posavina -- yes, 2nd Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that also had a chain of command, or a disciplined order to it, as any army would?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it ran from, in the chain of command, from the soldiers, or privates, all the way up to the top, to General Mladic, who was the chief commander, or the general in charge?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And between General Mladic and the soldiers, you had people of various ranks?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And within this 2nd Posavina Corps [sic], you had -- were the four detachments - the 1st Detachment, 2nd Detachment, 3rd, and the 4th - from Samac?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: There were already battalions in existence then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you had -- what used to be those detachments were now in that 2nd Posavina Brigade. And were you aware that Crni, or Dragan Djordjevic, was even made commander in May, of that whole brigade, of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, Dragan Djordjevic, whose nickname was Crni; one of the people from Serbia was named the commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I heard that he had been nominated, and then immediately following his nomination, I was wounded and I left. So I'm not fully familiar with that, because I sort of skipped over that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But before you were injured, you had heard that he had in fact been nominated to be the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: As a result, all the soldiers within the brigade had to answer up the line, eventually to Crni, or Dragan Djordjevic, if he took that position. Because he was the commander, you would have to do what he said.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: We had to carry out those tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in carrying out those tasks, the different soldiers in, whether it was the 17th Posavina Group - I'm sorry - the 2nd Posavina or the 17th Tactical Group, had to work -- had to follow their orders and work together, had to coordinate their activities when they're told to do so?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And as part of the coordination, you all had radios so you could communicate with each, or different groups had radios so you could communicate; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And let's just finish off with that one period of April 16th, 17th, 18th, and 19th. You said you saw the camouflage people out there.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You saw the tanks arrive, the JNA tanks?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: We saw one tank in the morning, after the dawn, by the silos. That's where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You saw one JNA tank, and as I said, you had radios. The radios, you used them with the same frequency so you could talk with each other?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have it, because I was not involved in establishing communication. I heard it from our commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The radios that the commanders were using had the same frequency so they could talk with each other and coordinate their activities?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Probably so, but I had nothing to do with communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I know you had nothing to do with it. I'm just saying that because -- for an army to function, you have to use the same radio frequency, obviously, as you know, having been in the military. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Probably so. I was a driver in the army, and again, had nothing to do with communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And all these different groups, whether it was the tank, the 1st Detachment, the 17th Detachment, the specials from Serbia, you were all coordinating and working together to fight the enemy; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: We did not command; we were issued orders, and we fought the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were issued orders and you were all working together, after being issued orders, to fight the enemy; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: There was no combat there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, you were working together, or you were coordinated to defend the city and be prepared to fight, then; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: In order to defend the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, like any other army, you got your orders and everyone was working together in a coordinated effort, which is the plan of operation of any army; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how the planning is done. I suppose that the Superior Command does the planning, and we simply had to carry out the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, following the orders, everyone had certain assignments to do, and they're coordinated, because everyone's doing a certain job or chore or assignment; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. PRESIDING OFFICER: Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Savic, perhaps there's a misunderstanding here or the question was not quite specific, the question of my colleague Prosecutor which had to do with combat. You said that on the -- that from the Croatian side, a shell was fired at the silo.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You also said there were skirmishes and occasional firing during the night between the 16th and 17th of April, in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the bunker was located by the bridge? Was there any firing from there directed at Samac?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Madam Presiding Officer --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: -- I did not raise --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I withdraw. I withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is what we mentioned. Is this your understanding of a combat operation? Is this combat?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. From the 17th on, was Samac shelled? Were shells landing?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. There was firing from Slavonia and from Prud.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: From the 17th on, was the front line established, the defensive front line around Samac? Or rather, were ... END OF RECORDING ... positions there set, facing enemy lines?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What do you personally know regarding the link between the SDS and the 17th Tactical Group? I would like to know whether the SDS in any way participated in operations of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: According to what I know, the SDS did not cooperate with the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What do you know about whether Blagoje Simic, as an individual, acted in cooperation with the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SAVIC
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that, but this was never mentioned. There were no rumours to this effect either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Savic. We've completed our examination. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you, Mr. Savic, for coming. You can go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. PRESIDING OFFICER: We'll start again at 10 to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.34 p.m

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Good afternoon, Mr. Nijemcevic. Would you please stand and take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. For the record, please tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Mitar, father's name Stojan, surname Nijemcevic. I was born on January 1st, 1963, in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you married, and do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: I am married. I have two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Have you completed secondary school of mechanical engineering in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You did your military service in the JNA, and you were in artillery rocket units and anti-air defences?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I served in Kraljevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Having completed your military service, you became a reservist, and your rank in the reserve is lieutenant, second lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is from the former JNA, and I have not been promoted since.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Immediately prior to the outbreak of armed conflict in the territory of Samac municipality in April 1992, you were the head of a building material warehouse in the village of Struke, near Prud? That is where your family home is too, in Struke, isn't it; that is where you lived?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, until the outbreak of the conflict I was there, and then in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During the state of war, having left Struke, just before the beginning of the conflict, or round about then - but you will explain that later for us - your house was destroyed, so actually, you're no longer living in Struke?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. My house was destroyed, so I'm now living in Samac, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You're living with your family and your wife's parents, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm working in a metal farm called Njegos, in Samac, producing metal, electrical equipment, boilers and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the period from mid-April 1992 up until the end of May 1992, you were a member of an intervention unit within the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You were wounded for the first time on the 27th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And for the second time, on the 12th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: After treatment was completed, you were found to be 70 per cent war disabled; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nijemcevic, before we move on to your testimony linked to a meeting that took place in your home, will you please, in a few sentences only, give us some background to this event and describe for us the situation in your village of Struke in the month of March, with respect to relations between Serbs and Croats, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Struke is a very small place, consisting of some 20 households. There were about 18 households and 20 houses -- no. I'm sorry. There were 20 households, of which two were Croat, 18 Serb. There was some tension between the parties, so that I felt that we were in jeopardy. On the one hand there was Odzak, and to the other side there was Prud, so that we were sort of closed in on both sides, so that two or three times a conflict occurred amongst us; actually, between the inhabitants of Struke and those of Dubica and Prud.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you notice any fortifications, weapons, on the river banks and in the immediate surroundings of Struke, in March?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since my house was right next to the main road, there was an embankment which protected the village from the flooding of the Bosna River, and along that embankment, just before the war, that is, in March, there were artillery weapons dug in by the Croat or Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Madam Presiding Officer, I just need to register my objection to this evidence. We are now straying. I've been waiting for us to get to the two topics that are clearly delineated in the filing that was the joint defence motion in respect of Rule 71. The filing was very specific. There are two topics mentioned, namely, whether or not Blagoje Simic discussed or mentioned the division of the municipality; and secondly, the presence of one of the Prosecution witnesses at a particular meeting and the circumstances under which the defendant Blagoje Simic appeared at that meeting. Those two topics have not yet been reached. We're now moving into an area regarding the fortifications and placing of arms by the Croatian forces. That is well outside, well outside, of the two topics, and I object to this evidence and submit that Mr. Pantelic should now direct the witness, having settled the witness and obtained the necessary personal details, directly into those two topics that are clearly delineated in the joint defence motion made in respect of Rule 71.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, in response to the Prosecution's submission, I believe that this short evidence with regard to the atmosphere in the village of Struke immediately prior to the meeting, which is actually the topic that we shall discuss in a few seconds, is necessary in order to know background of the situation by itself, and then we shall hear the explanation of this witness with regard to the discussion, so that meeting, presence of various persons, et cetera. So just for the record, that is my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Pantelic. If we could get on to the establishment of the checkpoints. We all know the evidence of the witness and how the meetings came about and the reason for the meetings. And then we can go directly to those two topics, and that will save time and also mean that the Prosecution won't be standing up and objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is indeed my intention, and in fact my next question after this explanation will be strictly focused to this particular meeting. So it's just an introduction, as I would say. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Di Fazio, are you moving to strike these portions you've just mentioned, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Nijemcevic, we are coming now to the event for which you have been called here to testify in the defence case for Blagoje Simic. During these proceedings, a certain episode was interpreted in a particular way. We would now like to hear from you what happened. My first question is: Could you tell us whether, in March - and you will tell us which part of March - in your house, in the village of Struke, a meeting was held. Was a meeting held in your house?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was, around mid-March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for convening that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of March, we had some unfortunate incidents caused by inhabitants of Dubica and some inhabitants of Prud. We are a very small locality. So they were afraid of the army, and we were a buffer for them. So they feared that if we left, the army would come in. And on two occasions, we had negotiated with them, but there was one access after another, and it became more and more difficult. And then this meeting was convened to calm the situation down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you say "they," do you mean the Croats?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And when you say "we," you mean the Serbs from Struke?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, some ten inhabitants. It's a very small hamlet, in fact. It was a hamlet attached to Prud.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nijemcevic, in that period of 1992, were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not, and I am not a member of any party today, nor do I intend to become one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you have never been a member of any party?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: That's right, and I believe I never will be a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: What was the motive for that meeting to be held in your house?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: My house has a rather specific position. It is somehow in a neutral position, along the line separating Prud and Dubica. And because there was a large enough room to receive several participants, or a number of participants. That was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please tell me now: If I understood you correctly - but please correct me if you feel I'm wrong - so you and the others decided to hold this joint meeting in order to deal with these ethnic tensions and problems that were present between the Serb and Croat populations?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't I who decided about that meeting, but somebody else, Milan Rakic, a man who was killed, probably in agreement with somebody called Matanovic. I think he was from Odzak. And there were also representatives of the Croats and of the Serbs, that means of Prud, Dubica, Vojskova, and Struke.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you were a kind of host of the meeting and not the initiator?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I was the host, yes, but I was really serving my guests with coffee and drinks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nijemcevic, will you try, though I know it was a long time ago, try and tell us now, with regard to the Serb representatives from the area, which persons attended that meeting. Slowly, for the record, so we can note down the surnames, if you remember, of course.

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember some surnames. I remember this Milan Rakic, from Novi Grad; I remember Rajko Djuric, I think his surname was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Truman, Truman. That was his nickname. He very briefly -- Miro --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: -- came in very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But among those who attended the meeting -- so you told us these two names. Can you remember anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Milic from Dubica, Ljubisa Djuric, and I think Sreten, and another man. I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So those were representing the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but for the purpose of an agreement, of an easing of tensions, things like that. The meeting itself was organised by this Milan Rakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now tell us, please: On the Croatian side, who do you remember attending that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: From Vojskova, there was this Matanovic. Actually, I think he's from Odzak. I think his name was Ivica and I think he was an officer. Then from Vojskova, Caktas [phoen]; and another one, Bono, known as Guda [phoen]. I don't know his surname. From Prud, there was Zoran Obrenovic; and another man, I think it was Anto Pepic. But these were more or less observers, actually. Because Ivica Matanovic, he really represented them at that meeting, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was he an officer? Did he have a military position?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: I think he was an officer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: And from Prud, did anyone attend?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: This Zoran Obrenovic and Anto Pepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was a Mijo, known as Mis, present too?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who was this Mijo?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: I think he was an officer in reserve too. I didn't know him very well, really. We were neighbours, that's true, but we didn't really know each other; we just said hello. I think the man is an active military man in the army of the Federation now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So those were the persons that you listed as Croats, representing the other side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Do you know a person by the name of Blaz Paradzik?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Where is he from?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: The man is from Prud.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you know him personally? Would you see him often?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: I would see him. We didn't socialise, we didn't have any particular contacts, but I do know the man. Why? Why? Has he done anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, he says that he attended that meeting. That's why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Blaz? No. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So my question now: Did Blaz Paradzik attend the meeting that you are now describing, held in March 1992, in the presence of all these people?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you explain briefly the topics discussed at that meeting. What did you talk about, and what conclusions were reached, if any?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: The main and only topic, in fact, was to ease tensions and avoid excesses, and for us to be allowed passage from our village to Samac, and vice versa, to Odzak, because we couldn't get out anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you say "we," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: I mean the Serb side. I mean the villagers of Struke.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what was the position of the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian side kept repeating that if the villagers of Struke move out, the army would come in, and they were afraid of the army. And in the end, the agreement was that they would allow women and children to leave, and some 10 to 12 men that there were, aged between 15 and 70, those 12 of them, should stay behind as some sort of guarantors. And that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So I understand that the women, children, and the elderly Serbs from the village were allowed by the Croats to cross to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but they succeeded the third time they tried.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So how long did this take, roughly?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of March until sometime at the end of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't object, but that evidence is unclear, and I suggest it should be clarified. Is the witness saying that these negotiations were ongoing throughout March, leading to the departure of these people throughout the period of March, on frequent occasions? That will be necessary for the Trial Chamber to have a good understanding of what this witness is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nijemcevic, I understood you to say that after two attempts -- at the third attempt it was agreed that the women and children could leave. Did they all leave in different periods or all in one group? Could you indicate that? When you said the third time round --

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: The meeting that was held at my home was the meeting at which it was agreed that the children and the elderly and women could leave. There were some sort of informal meetings and discussions on the road two or three times, and after two or three attempts, the women and children were still not allowed to leave. And throughout the month of March, there were no more meetings, but simply two men from Prud, who were very fair and correct, they had the greatest merit for the final permission that was given to the women and children to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: And when did this happen in relation to the meeting? When did they actually leave? After the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Talking about that, your wife and children -- I don't know whether you had children in those days.

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When did they cross over into Samac?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Before the meeting. Before the meeting, across the Bosna River, by boat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In a boat. Why didn't they use the bridge leading to Samac?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: It was not possible to reach the bridge, because there were checkpoints along the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who held those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: The so-called reserve policemen, that is, the locals from Prud. We reached the bridge; however, they turned us back, on the pretext that if we left, this army would come in. That was their excuse all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you consider yourself to be some sort of hostages?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, something to that effect. When you don't have freedom of passage and you can't leave, that's what it is, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Madam Presiding Officer, I object to that last -- the content of that last answer. I'd move for that to be struck out. We're now moving beyond attendance at the meetings that are described in the summary and to the actual substance of events in the area of Prud and Bosanski Samac during the month of March. The summary is very specific, very, very clear and very specific: It's those two meetings in the presence of people. That's what we're -- that's what the summary is about and that's the areas that I submit that Mr. Pantelic should confine himself to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No comment from the Defence side. I will proceed with the other topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nijemcevic, in your previous answer you mentioned Miro Tadic as having come by. Tell me first: Do you know Mr. Miroslav Tadic, known as Brko?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He was my teacher in secondary school. He taught -- he gave practical training lessons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell us, in connection with that meeting, what his role was. Did he attend the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. Tadic dropped in for five to ten minutes. He said hello to Rakic and Matanovic, he had his coffee and left. Now, where he went, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who did he come with to your home? Did he come alone or in somebody's company?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: No. He came alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know Dr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What can you say about his presence at that meeting, Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Simic came maybe five or six hours after Tadic, in the afternoon. He stayed 15 to 20 minutes. The talks were almost over. Again, the man exchanged greetings, had his coffee, and left. Now, where he left, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: While he was present in your house, did Dr. Blagoje Simic say anything to the effect that Samac municipality needed to be divided: a part should belong to the Serbs and another part to other peoples? Did he say something like that at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't. Dr. Simic, when he arrived, he said hello and he said, jokingly, that we should come to some sort of agreement so that problems should be avoided. But there was no mention of any divisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did Dr. Blagoje Simic on that occasion mention the founding of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: No, though I'm not in any party, but on that occasion, no such things were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did Dr. Blagoje Simic at that meeting speak about the expulsion of non-Serbs from Samac on the part of the Serbs and as a result of their policies?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, we wouldn't have let him say anything like that, because of the position we were in, and he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did Dr. Blagoje Simic on that occasion speak of discrimination towards other ethnic groups, towards Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: No, that was not the topic of discussion at all. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Pantelic, you have two more minutes to finish, because of the objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I just finished my examination-in-chief. Thank you, Madam Presiding Officer. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nijemcevic. I've finished my examination. The Prosecutor will have a few questions for you now, after which I will have some more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Nijemcevic, my name is Di Fazio. I've just got a few questions for you. I won't be long.

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Because of the position of your house, it was a good idea to hold these meetings there, between Croatians who lived in Prud and Serbs who lived in Struke?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And in fact, I believe Struke and Prud are, although separate villages, or small towns, are in fact -- they looked as if they're linked because the buildings are clustered close together. To someone who didn't know the ethnicity of the inhabitants, it might look as if it's all part of the one small town; is that a fair assessment of the way it looks?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
