utterances.text: No. Prud and Struke are along the border dividing two places, and there is an interspace of about 1.000 or 1.500 metres, dividing Struke and Prud.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. Okay. Thank you. But in any event, the best place to hold the meeting was at your house?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Not the best place, but this was some sort of a crossroads, of a rallying point centre, and everybody came there, so it was the most favourable spot from that point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. You say it was a rallying point and a centre and everyone came there. Do I take it that in those troubled times, in early 1992, quite a few meetings were held there?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: No. One meeting was held in my house, and there was a sort of an informal meeting which was held outside, in the street, on the road, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Near your house?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, some 100 or 200 metres away from my house, practically in the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke of the attempts to reach agreement with the Croats from Prud regarding the departure of Serbs from Struke, and you said that on the third attempt there was an agreement reached. Does that mean that on at least three occasions you spoke to each other, the groups, the Serbs and the Croats, regarding this issue?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakic talked with them on our behalf. We personally did not. It was Mr. Rakic who conducted this talk with Mr. Matanovic, who probably was the representative of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And meetings were held in other houses in the area of Struke, and maybe even Prud, regarding this issue, this matter?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: No, not in Struke. No other meetings were held at Struke. Probably somewhere in the area or some other area, some other houses. This is something that I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, on the day of this meeting that you've given detailed evidence about, how many men in all would you say were present in your house?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, a rough estimate would be about 20 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. And that would -- I assume all made up of either Struke residents or Prud residents.

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: From Struke, there were four or five people. From Odzak, Dubica, Prud, Vojskova, there were more of them. There were more people from the Croatian and Muslim side. There were two men from the Croat side, from Odzak, whom I didn't know, but there were more people from the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And no doubt this was a reasonably tense time for you because you had to host them, look after these men, make sure that they were all looked after and they could carry on the business of trying to sort out this issue.

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. Perhaps I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were hosting the meeting and you had to look after the needs of these men who were gathered there?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any specific needs to look after. I just made them coffee and served a drink, as I would entertain any other guests in my house, whether I was the host or anybody else in the household.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And the house, I take it, was crowded with 20 or so men?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And Blaz Paradzik, you didn't know him very well, did you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I know. I've heard your evidence. I know that you knew him. But you didn't know him very well, did you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what you mean exactly when you say "very well." We didn't socialise. We would just say hello to each other, nothing more than that. We didn't have a -- we were not on close terms, but I know his face and I know how he looks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting you don't. And those times were fairly troubled times, weren't they, fairly tense times, for you personally and also for the inhabitants of Prud and Struke, and in fact the whole area?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: I think that the times were much harder of the villagers of the village of Struke than those in Prud because we were only 10 or 12 households. The tensions were mounting, as is normal in war conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You can't tell us the names of each and every one of those 20 men. You can tell us some of the men who were there. Is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as regards those from the villages which were near my own village, I know those people. And also on the Odzak municipality and the Posavska Mahala area and Svilaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know the people well enough, and I couldn't remember their names. This is an area which is a bit off. It is some 20 kilometres away from my own village, and I didn't go there much, so I didn't know the people well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. And it seems that the people who were present at the meeting, it wasn't a static group; it was -- people were coming and going; at least, Miro Tadic and Blagoje Simic came briefly and left?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Nobody came in a compact group. These two men, Matanovic and Rakic, were negotiating each on behalf of their people, and others came and went. And no, they did not come in compact groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's right. People were coming and going, and coming to see how the meeting was going and how it was proceeding. It's not as if 20 men arrived all at once and left all at once; people were coming and going.

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. It wasn't that 20 of them came together. They kept coming within a space of perhaps an hour. But they did all leave together. Dr. Blagoje just dropped in for a while, and he left before the meeting ended. There was a slight incident between Mr. Rajko Djuric and Mr. Matanovic. They had an altercation of sorts. And the meeting was over at that point, so that everybody dispersed. And afterwards, Mile Rakic, after a couple of days, that is, came and told us that the vulnerable categories of people - women and children - could go, could leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for explaining that. Well, in those circumstances, do you think you might be mistaken when you say that Blaz Paradzik wasn't there, if people are coming and going and some of the people are strangers, and it's 10 or 11 years ago? Do you think you might have made a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I know exactly who was there from Prud, because these were people that I went to school to accept for this papage [phoen]. And I know my generation well. Blaz is a bit older than me or perhaps my age. I'm not quite sure. But I knew him. I couldn't have made that mistake, because I was right by the door, so I saw practically everyone who came in and went out, and I was also there to be near the kitchen, in order to be able to serve the coffee, so I saw all the going in and out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. Very well. What did Miro Tadic do at the meeting? I know he came and had coffee and was only there for five to ten minutes. That's what you said. Is that all that he did at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: That is all. In fact, we didn't know that Miro Tadic had come. We were surprised. He just dropped in for 10 to 15 minutes, had a coffee and a glass of brandy, and he left. I think that Miro Tadic either went to stay with his family down in Novi Grad, for lunch or -- I don't know where he went from there. But it is possible, seeing that that house is by the road, by the main road, it is possible that he went down there to stay with his relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know him very well, or did you know him very well in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: I knew him from school as a teacher. He was a practical instruction teacher. We were not on very close terms, nor did we meet often, or socialise. I just knew the man by sight, but not -- we were not very close. I know that he was a good teacher, that he liked to crack a joke; not much more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sure. And in those circumstances, of course, he obviously, plainly, was not coming to visit you; he was coming to see what was happening at the meeting. Right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know what was the reason why he came to the meeting. As I said before, we were surprised to see him there, because that man had never even dropped in my store before, let alone my house. So we were really surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. Naturally. And that must mean, therefore, that he knew of the meeting going on, and he came to the meeting to see what was happening at the meeting, not to visit you. He wasn't a friend of yours who would drop in at the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection. Calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Madam Presiding Officer, I think the witness is in a position to comment on the purpose of the -- of Mr. Tadic's presence at the meeting, or at least to be able to negate personal visit as a reason for his attendance at the meeting, and it's that negation that I'm interested in, and I'll therefore proceed with the question, and the Trial Chamber will eventually rule on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, this witness cannot know why the other person is coming or what was the reasons. Maybe the proper way would be to rephrase questions or to follow some more appropriate questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll approach it in the negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You can be sure, can't you, that he wasn't coming there to visit you personally; he had never done that before?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I tell you: I don't know why he came there, why Miro came there. I cannot give you a reply, because I really don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, what about Blagoje Simic? Was he a close personal friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Had he ever visited you at your house?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: No, he hadn't, not ever before. That was the only time that he came by, and that was late in the afternoon. He -- Miro was there for 10 to 15 minutes, and the meeting -- which was about 10.00 or 11.00, and Blagoje then dropped in sometime in the afternoon, about 5.00 or 6.00 p.m. And he talked more to Mr. Rakic and Mr. Matanovic than anybody else; what about, I don't know. And as for territorial divisions or a Serbian municipality, I can guarantee you with my life that that was not a topic of this meeting, and Blagoje contributed nothing of the sort to the meeting. After Blagoje had left, there was this small falling out between Mr. Rajko [phoen] and Mr. Matanovic, and the meeting ended abruptly the way it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You are absolutely certain, aren't you - this is your position, cast-iron, guaranteed, clear certainty - that they arrived at different times, even though, of course, the meeting happened 11 years ago and people were coming and going all day long?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: I am, precisely. Miro came first, there for 10 to 15 minutes, roughly about 10.00 or 11.00, and Blagoje came later, in the afternoon, as I've described.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. And of course, no doubt you could tell us the precise times of all the other people who dropped in as well.

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: No, not the precise times, but I could tell you who arrived first. Mr. Matanovic and Mr. Rakic, for instance, arrived first, the two of them. They were up there by my store, and after a meeting of a group of about ten people had assembled, then they all came to the house. And then all of the rest came in intervals, from the morning hours -- in intervals, from the morning hours, about 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning, to 4.00 or 5.00 or 6.00 in the afternoon. I don't know when the meeting exactly ended, but it was in the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: However, one thing is absolutely certain: You have perfect clarity of memory as far as the fact that both Tadic and Simic, Blagoje Simic, arrived separately?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is 1.000 per cent so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's very impressive. Thank you very much. Now, Mr. Blagoje Simic was, of course, at that time a leading community figure, wasn't he, because he was the president of the SDS in the area? He was a politician of some rank, wouldn't you say?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I primarily know Blagoje as a doctor, and I'm not engaged in politics or involved in it in any way. I'm not affiliated to any party. I'm not interested in the subject, in politics, at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for letting us know that. However, I'm not actually asking you about your interests, whether you're interested in politics or not. I'm not asking you that. What I'm asking you is this: Blagoje Simic was a well-known political figure in the area. He was president of the SDS, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know Blagoje Simic as a physician. Whether he was the SDS president, that I'm unable to tell you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: His party affiliation was of no interest to me. That's what I'm saying. So I don't know whether he was the president of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So your evidence is that you don't know what reputation he held in the community, you don't know how well known he was. All you know is that he was a doctor, is that right, a doctor who lived in Bosanski Samac, a simple country doctor living in Bosanski Samac? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is how I view him. And whether he wielded any authority with other people, that I don't know. For me, he was just an ordinary person, an ordinary doctor. As for authority, I hold him in high esteem as a professional and as a physician, and not as a political personage. I don't know him as a political personage, as a political figure, because I was myself a member of no party, so -- and I thereby was not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you concerned - sorry - were you surprised at the presence of this doctor at this meeting involving politics and local tensions? I mean, he was just a doctor who worked in Bosanski Samac. You didn't know anything about his political background and you didn't know him personally. You must have been bewildered as to what he was doing in your house.

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: I was bewildered, because -- and he probably had relations with other people that he had to discuss. It was just by dint of circumstances that this happened to be in my house. I was surprised myself to see him, because I had never had any contact with the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So if I suggested to you that, in fact, Blagoje Simic was an extremely well-known politician in the area, that the fact that he was known to be president of the SDS in the area was a fact known to everyone in that house, including yourself, and that he was an influential man, you would disagree with me?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot agree with your contention as regards politics and the SDS. I'm in no party. I'm not in politics. Whether he was held in high esteem or not, I don't know that. That depends on the viewer, on whose eyes were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. And as far as the creation of the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac, at the time of the meeting, were you aware that it had been created and declared?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: No. No, really not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So you can't tell us if that was a fact that was widely known, at least in the Serb community?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: It was a fact that was not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. And just finally: If I suggested to you that you're not being truthful when you say that Blaz Paradzik was not there, you would disagree with me?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: I told you. I told you that that man was not present at the meeting, and I listed the people who attended it. So I see no connection between Blaz Paradzik and this whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But you know what my position is, so you can tell me if you agree or disagree. That's all I'm doing. And I suggest to you that, in fact, Blaz Paradzik was there; I suggest to you that Truman and Tadic and Blagoje Simic arrived together; and I suggest to you that Blagoje Simic did address the meeting on the dismemberment of the existing municipalities. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: I disagree. I do not agree at all. This was not at all the topic of the meeting. I told you: Tadic, Professor Blagoje, and Truman did not come together. Mr. Matanovic and Mr. Rakic arrived, and Truman came a bit before Miro, and Blagoje arrived the last. Truman was somewhere, reportedly in Samac, and I don't know where exactly, and he was a bit drunk. This is actually what caused the incident, because he said that he was sorry that the meeting had started before him, and then Rakic start quarrelling with him, and there was a row, and then he started quarrelling with Matanovic, so that the meeting ended abruptly, in the way I've described.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I have no further questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nijemcevic, let's clarify just a few things for the sake of the record. You've mentioned, both when examined by me and by the Prosecutor, that there was a certain Matanovic present there. However, when answering the Prosecutor's questions, you did not indicate Matanovic's first name so let us just state clearly first and last name of that person attending the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Ivica Matanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The following question: Did you spend your entire childhood and youth in Struke?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 80 per cent of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You know Blaz Paradzik from Prud?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Since what time have you known him?

utterances.speaker: MITAR NIJEMCEVIC
utterances.text: I've known him since I was 15 or 18, roughly speaking, but I know him well. I know him well. We were not very close, we didn't socialise, but I know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How old were you in March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you, Mr. Nijemcevic, for coming and giving your deposition today. It's concluded and you can go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome. Thank you. DEFENCE COUNSEL: [Interpretation] I would like to suggest the following: We have two witnesses left for Monday, and could we perhaps start at 10.00? Because of the witness who is coming in the morning, I would need to speak to Mr. Pantelic, and since we have only two witnesses, I believe it wouldn't be a problem if we started at 10.00. PRESIDING OFFICER: That's what I wanted to suggest. We'll start at 10.00 on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: at 3.16 p.m., to be followed by the Trial which will reconvene on Monday, the 10th day of February, 2003, at 10.00 a.m.
